blurb: Convert, compress, and edit video/audio files from the command line.

flags.label: Input File
flags.plainEnglish: The video or audio file you want to process.

flags.label: Resize / Scale
flags.plainEnglish: Shrinks the video's resolution. Smaller = faster processing and smaller file size.

flags.label: Video Quality
flags.plainEnglish: Lower number = better quality, bigger file. 18-28 is normal. 23 is a good default.

flags.label: Encoding Speed
flags.plainEnglish: Slower presets compress more efficiently (smaller file at same quality) but take longer to run.

flags.label: Remove Video (audio only)
flags.plainEnglish: Strips out the video track entirely — use this to extract just the audio.

flags.label: Remove Audio
flags.plainEnglish: Strips out the audio track, keeping only video (e.g. for silent GIF-style clips).

flags.label: Start Time
flags.plainEnglish: Skip to this timestamp before processing (e.g. 00:00:30 for 30 seconds in). Leave blank to start from the beginning.

flags.label: Duration
flags.plainEnglish: How long a clip to process, e.g. 00:00:10 for 10 seconds. Leave blank to go to the end of the file.

flags.label: Simple Quality (alt to CRF)
flags.plainEnglish: Alternate quality control, mainly used for image/GIF output. Lower = better quality. Rarely needed if you're already using Video Quality (CRF). Disabled by default — enable to override.

flags.label: Frame Rate
flags.plainEnglish: Frames per second in the output. Disabled by default, which keeps the source's original frame rate. Enable to override.

flags.label: Audio Sample Rate
flags.plainEnglish: Audio quality setting in Hz. 44100 is the standard for music, 48000 for video.

flags.label: Audio Bitrate
flags.plainEnglish: Higher bitrate = better audio quality, bigger file. 192k is a solid default for most uses.

flags.label: Output File Name
flags.plainEnglish: The name for the finished file. Saved automatically to your CLIFace output folder.

presets.name: Compress video for email
presets.description: Shrinks file size while keeping it watchable — good for attaching to emails or Slack.

presets.name: Convert video to MP3
presets.description: Extracts just the audio track from a video file.
presets.testNote: Relies on ffmpeg inferring the mp3 encoder (libmp3lame) from the .mp3 output extension rather than an explicit -c:a flag. This is usually reliable but version-dependent — verify with a real run during Milestone 1 testing, add explicit -c:a libmp3lame if inference ever fails.

presets.name: Extract a short clip
presets.description: Cuts a section out of a longer video without re-encoding the whole thing.

presets.name: High quality archive copy
presets.description: Keeps quality as close to the original as possible, larger file size.

presets.name: Small file for messaging apps
presets.description: Aggressively compresses for platforms with strict size limits (e.g. WhatsApp, Discord).

notes.-vf:scale: This is a synthetic flag name (not a real ffmpeg flag) representing one specific use of -vf. Real ffmpeg -vf accepts arbitrary filter chains; v1 only exposes the 'scale' filter as a friendly dropdown. buildArgsArray must expand -vf:scale into the real ['-vf', 'scale=1280:-1'] pair via argTemplate, not pass '-vf:scale' literally to spawn.
notes.output: Not a real flag — it's the positional output filename argument ffmpeg expects last. Schema-to-args logic needs to treat 'output' as a special positional field, appended at the end of the args array, not as a '-flag value' pair.
notes.convention:unset-enum: Any optional enum flag includes an explicit sentinel value (unsetSentinel, e.g. '__unset__') as one of its enum options, always rendered as the first/default choice with a label like 'Default (no change)'. buildArgsArray skips the flag entirely — including any argTemplate expansion — when the selected value equals unsetSentinel. This is the ONLY way to represent 'don't pass this flag' for enum types; never rely on default: null, since there's no UI affordance for null in a dropdown.
notes.convention:unset-number: Any optional number flag is paired with optional: true and enabled: false by default. The numeric input stays disabled/greyed out in the form until the user explicitly enables it. buildArgsArray skips the flag entirely when enabled is false, regardless of what value sits in the (disabled) input. This is the numeric-type equivalent of convention:unset-enum.
notes.convention:conflicts-symmetric: conflictsWith is treated as symmetric by the validator regardless of which flag declares it — if A lists B, the form disables B whenever A is set and vice versa, even though only A's schema entry mentions the relationship. Schema authors declare each conflicting pair on exactly one side, never both, to avoid drift between two hand-maintained copies of the same fact. Ordering rule: declare the conflict on the 'primary'/basic flag's entry (e.g. -crf, not -q:v), so the canonical declaration always lives on the flag a user is more likely to touch first.
notes.convention:always-on-defaults: Not every advanced flag follows the unset-sentinel/disabled-by-default pattern. -b:a has a real default (192k) and is always passed, even if the user never touches it — deliberate, since audio bitrate benefits from an explicit value and 192k is a safe universal default. The unset/disabled pattern is reserved for flags where 'not passing this at all' has distinct real meaning to ffmpeg (e.g. -ar unset lets ffmpeg keep the source's native sample rate, which isn't the same as picking one explicitly).
notes.convention:explicit-kind: Every flag declares its own kind (standard | boolean | templated | positional) as an explicit schema field. buildArgsArray dispatches on this declared value directly — it never infers kind from other signals (e.g. flag === 'output', or presence of argTemplate), because inference just relocates the same ad hoc per-flag branching into a second hidden function instead of eliminating it. Schema authors for future tools must set kind explicitly on every flag; there is no default.
notes.known-limitation:flag-ordering: buildArgsArray outputs non-positional flags in schema-definition order. ffmpeg is order-sensitive in ways this schema doesn't encode — most notably, -ss placed before -i triggers fast input-seeking, while -ss placed after -i (the current schema order, since -i is defined first) falls back to slower filter-based seeking. Both produce correct output; only speed differs. This is a deliberate v1 simplification, not a bug: schema-definition order is treated as good enough for v1's flag set. Flagged as a known limitation for a v1.1 pass — a future version could add an explicit 'order' or 'position' field per flag if seek performance on the 'Extract a short clip' preset becomes a real complaint, rather than relying on schema-definition order as an implicit ordering mechanism.
notes.convention:unset-string: A string-type flag whose resolved value is the empty string is treated as unset. The actual enforcement is a blanket rule in isSkipped: any flag (regardless of unsetSentinel) with resolved.value === '' or undefined is skipped — this catch-all is what does the real work for -ss/-t, not the unsetSentinel: '' declaration on those flags, which is redundant with it in this schema (no flag here needs a legitimately meaningful empty string). The unsetSentinel: '' fields are set mainly for documentation clarity / consistency with the enum convention. Do not remove the blanket empty-string catch-all thinking it's dead code shadowed by the sentinel check — it is the mechanism actually skipping -ss/-t today.
notes.convention:required-missing: A flag marked required: true that resolves to no value at all (undefined/empty, no schema default) throws a RequiredFieldError rather than silently producing an incomplete command (e.g. an ffmpeg invocation missing -i entirely). Same reasoning as ConflictError: this path should be structurally unreachable if the form renderer enforces required fields, so a thrown error surfaces a renderer bug loudly instead of silently shipping a broken command.
notes.convention:vn-conflict-scope: -vn's conflictsWith originally listed -crf and -preset alongside -vf:scale and -an. Removed -crf/-preset: confirmed real ffmpeg behavior is that passing an unused encoder option (e.g. -crf/-preset with no video stream to encode, because -vn removed it) produces a non-fatal debug-level warning ('Codec AVOption ... has not been used for any stream') and the command still succeeds. This is 'irrelevant', not 'conflicting' — unlike -vf:scale, where filtering a video stream that doesn't exist is a real error condition, not just an ignored option. Also structurally necessary: -crf/-preset have no unsetSentinel and are always-on-default flags (per convention:always-on-defaults), so they have no valid 'inactive' state a force-reset could ever put them into — treating them as conflicts here would have made the 'Convert video to MP3' preset (which sets -vn but doesn't mention -crf/-preset) permanently unresolvable, since those two flags are always active by construction.
